Gene assessments – what you need to understand  

Clinical Evidence Based Genetics  

Alzheimer’s illness, diabetes and mental health genetic assessments have all been highlighted as fields to be cautious of in the long-anticipated Genomics in General Practice handbook from the RACGP.  

The handbook has been in the making for years and is the first major document of guidance for general practitioners since a 2007 resource by the now obsolete Biotechnology Australia.  

As the expense of genetic and genomic assessments has become more reasonable, and private firms are promoting directly to customers with often overstated assertions of advantages, the specialists behind the handbook were mindful to emphasize assessments for conditions such as Alzheimer’s and mental disorders which patients most frequently showed interest and wanted to discuss with their GP.  

Assessments for pharmacogenomics and MTHFR were other fields of worry, with the writers advising doctors there was little if any proof to back their usefulness in routine clinical practice.  

“While many of the medications commonly prescribed in general practice (e.g. warfarin, fluoxetine) are affected by genetic variation, there is presently no clear guidance in Australia about the use of pharmacogenomic assessments,” the writers said.  

Interest in MTHFR assessments was another area presently “blowing up” in genomics, with alternative practitioners requesting assessments for a range of chronic diseases, explained author Professor Sylvia Metcalfe, honorary fellow with Murdoch Children’s Research Institute.  

These types of dubious assessments were behind a rising number of individuals taking folate or vitamin B12 supplementation unnecessarily, she added.  

The guide offers a careful approach and outlines the potential ethical and practical advice GPs can provide their patients, which includes warnings over potential privacy and credibility issues, as well as implications for health and life insurance.  

While the guide writers have taken a quite conservative approach, it was one GPs were likely to endorse, Professor Metcalfe, also an honorary professor in pediatrics at the University of Melbourne, said.  

“We’ve been quite clear that although a lot of things are promoted in a very strong way, much of that assessment is not predictively beneficial.”  

The booklet was crafted to be easy to navigate and includes a short few practice points at the beginning of each condition’s chapter to summarize the current understanding.  

For example, the section on autism spectrum disorder explains that referral to a pediatrician will usually involve a genetics evaluation of the child providing a specific diagnosis in 30 to 40% of instances.  

It adds that GPs “can order a chromosome microarray (CMA) at the point of referral to a pediatrician in order to hasten this process”.  

The booklet highlights when to order assessments, when not to, and when to refer on to experts and genetic counselors.  

The sections on familial cancer and prenatal assessments are very clear about the value of assessments in these situations.  

Professor Metcalfe mentioned she hoped GPs would familiarize themselves with the indications for reproductive carrier assessments and other reproductive genomic assessments.  

The guide includes information on how to take a comprehensive family history and draw a family history pedigree.  

Women and their partners planning a pregnancy, or who are already pregnant, should have an extensive family history documented. Recognized carriers or parents-to-be with a family history of a genetic disorder should be made aware of and offered assessments and referral to expert services, it states.  

The guide also provides rebuttals to some commonly held misconceptions in the community, such as the notion that having a gene for a disease means that the patient will inevitably develop the disease.  

“If the gene variant shows variable penetrance (i.e. penetrance less than 100%), the risk of disease can be uncertain.”  

Other disorders discussed in the new guide include autism spectrum disorder, cystic fibrosis, developmental delay and intellectual disability, fragile X syndrome and associated conditions, familial hypercholesterolaemia, haemoglobinopathies, hereditary haemochromatosis, hereditary thrombophilia, melanoma, neurofibromatosis type 1, sudden arrhythmic death syndrome, chromosome microarray and newborn screening.  

The Genomics in General Practice guide can be found on the RACGP website.

Cynthia Reports - Friday  
I was at Sacred Heart today from 10:15 until 3:00. I have all my pre-surgery taken care of. I have now had 16 vials of blood extracted since August 22. I would make a good pincushion. If I pass my echocardiogram on Monday (which I feel is no issue) I will have my operation next Thursday. I have to be there by 5:30 I think surgery will be about 8.  

If the cancer has not spread the surgery should last 3-4 hours. I would be in the hospital 3-4 days and I wouldn't have to have chemo. This is what I am praying for.  

If the cancer has disseminated the surgery could last as long as 10 hours. I would be in the hospital up to 10 days and would have to have chemo. Chemo would probably last 2-3 weeks but could last up to 16 weeks.  

I will lose a lot of blood and will need to have a blood transfusion. He has ordered 8 units of blood but I should only need 4. I might have to stay in ICU the first night.  

I have a germ cell tumor. He didn't write ovarian in front of it but I think it should be. It is one of two sorts. Dr. DeCesare wrote it out for me but it is hard to read his handwriting. I looked it up online and I think he meant endodermal sinus tumor or dysgermionma. He said it is rare and fast growing.

When Firefly and school intersect  
Wednesday, March 16, 2005  

I'm sure most of us wish we could incorporate Firefly into a regular conversation, but that chance seldom occurs. I don't think I've deliberated anything Firefly associated outside of the various sites and enthusiasts I've encountered. The nearest I've ever arrived was in my Humanities class when someone mentioned Buffy in a presentation.  

Imagine my astonishment when Firefly was introduced in my English class. Okay, so it was my sci-fi English class, but it was still cool. My prof was discussing space operas, fundamentally narratives that are westerns in space, and started to present some examples. Naturally he referenced Star Trek, but to my pleasure he also referred to Firefly. I think quite literally my heart skipped a beat. In essence he stated that Firefly was captivating, as small as it was, but humble. And humble in the sense that when compared to the space operas, the show was less grand. From that little bit I couldn't ascertain if he had been impressed by the show, but clearly he was acquainted with it.  

Which led me to start pondering about crafting my next essay on Firefly. If my prof is familiar with the concept of the show, I really don't have to clarify it to him and that, I'd presume, would be the challenging part. I was considering I could contrast Firefly with one of the space operas we've studied in class. Contrast what? Well, I hadn't reached that far yet. But personally, it's still a fascinating thought. I could genuinely write about something that I know very well and actually sound intelligent.  

I should probably consider a topic before I get any happier. But how often do you get to mix Firefly and academia?

Naturally combine it in? Not frequently. But as an English instructor, I've succeeded to integrate it a few times. Tell your instructor he's definitely awesome! :D Get him on the site here, too.

Marketing SaaS to Corporations Means Your Site is Sovereign

Your site is the unsung hero in your advertising mix. Always available, it stands there waiting to be examined by your prospective clients. Welcoming them in, and giving them the data they need to know to make the shrewdest of choices – to select you. Are you giving your site the focus it merits?


12%—that’s how much of your customer’s total attention you as a provider have across the entire B2B buying journey.”

Research by CEB, now owned by Gartner

Open 24/7

Your clients are visiting your site and your rivals’ sites. They are examining everything before they complete a form. In fact, according to Triblio’s study 45% of purchasers have been on your site multiple times over 90 days before filling out a single form. I’ve seen this with our clients’ patrons. When you look back at the path of those who convert, multiple individuals in their organization have gone to the site numerous times over the 3 – 9 months it usually takes to seal a deal. Significantly more times than prospects who do not convert.

Site visits are a sign. In fact, according to Triblio, accounts with 2 or more distinct visitors convert more frequently than those with just one visitor, which makes sense considering buying committees in corporations. Knowing that multiple stakeholders are visiting your site makes it all the more crucial to pay attention to web messaging. Remember, your site is open for business 24/7, not just to your known leads but also to unknown key decision makers and influencers.

That signifies your site must be user-friendly, and possess the correct, updated data that best reflects your value proposition and advantages while aligning with what your client is seeking. Sounds straightforward, right? Then why are so many company sites a hot mess?

Get Your Site Messaging Correct

We've discovered the main issue in getting the messaging correct is ensuring the writer is collaborating with the actual decision maker - and there is only one decision maker. Click To Tweet That individual has to have the authority to make all final choices on messaging. That indicates if the CEO assigns someone to review, modify, and approve content, the CEO can’t come later and say it’s all incorrect. In other words, site messaging usually needs to be led by someone in the C-Suite with the authority to support the opinion. Our most successful messaging projects have been the writer collaborating directly with the CEO, in partnership with our content strategist. The strategist ensures the tone is where it needs to be and the CTAs are targeted, the writer gets the messaging correct, and the CEO ensures all key points are addressed.


Opinions from Thought Leaders

“Let’s say that a person can locate your site easily, have you enhanced the user experience, so they can collect the information they need effortlessly and swiftly? Is the content you are offering them pertinent and does it improve the user’s perception of your service? Are you guiding them to the conversion endpoint with click-through actions? If you do not have an active campaign for search engine optimization, search engine marketing, conversion rate optimization and content based marketing, then the answer to these inquiries may be a No. Yes, you have a site, but are you employing it to its maximum capability? In today’s information-driven world, to surpass the competition and enhance your conversion rates, it’s vital to have a well-optimized site.” Arin Adamson, Head of Web Development, Digital Reach Agency


“Your site is really the only location you can govern your buyer’s experience. By directing them there, you’re then able to cultivate their experience and create a clear path to KPI conversions (because we know the path to enterprise sales is a lengthy one). Maximizing the site visit is crucial to both grab their attention and their information to ensure that you can nurture them along their route to purchase.” – Maureen Jann



“If your site copy is attempting to appeal to multiple buyers, you’re destined to have a perplexing, ineffective message. That’s why it’s essential to outline clear paths for your different audience segments, so you can customize your copy for each of them, without confusing the other users on your site.” – Erika Heald




“On your site, you have the capacity to control your message and the buyer’s experience. The first impression they have on your site can make or break the sale, no matter how many emails you send them for a personalized demo of your product. Make the most of your real estate, and check your analytics to adjust performance when necessary.” Berrak Sarikaya



Clarity of Vision

Designing by committee rarely works out well. While writers work better in teams to produce a quality product, designers typically prefer to operate alone. The same applies to the group that assesses the site. If a single individual is executing a vision, then the site has a higher chance of achieving that vision. If the site has to satisfy all opinions, well, it will likely conclude as something that pleases everyone, while satisfying no one. Boring. Uninspiring. Just as a single decision maker is crucial for copy, it’s essential for design as well. It doesn’t need to be the same individual, and often isn’t. Writers who obsess over every syllable rarely lose sleep over design, and vice versa. Leave everyone to their strengths, and trust your team to execute.

Your future clients visiting your site will appreciate you.

Saturday, January 29, 2011  

Attention Span Reexamined  

There have been countless formulas proposed for measuring the attention span of children, teenagers and adults.  

Some modern researchers endorse evaluating children’s attention spans by multiplying chronological age by 3 to 5 minutes for each year of age. Others have determined the human attention span at a maximum of 20 - 22 minutes of learning time for later adolescence and adulthood.  

Still other child development researchers have concluded that a child’s attention span is usually equivalent in minutes to the chronological age of that young lad or lass.  

However, from collaborating with educators, parents, and children over the past four decades, the following instructional attention spans seem most precise and beneficial.  

Attention Span: Under Ideal Conditions*  
• Between ages 2 and 3 children have an attention span varying from 3-4 minutes  
• When children commence Kindergarten (approximately age 5), attention spans ascend to a maximum of 5 to 10 consecutive minutes  
• Between ages 6 and 8, the maximum duration for focused attention, during instructional time, can extend to 15-20 minutes when children are involved in a single learning task.  
• From age 9 to 12, the best approximations of an adolescent’s “focused attention” do not surpass 22 to 35 minutes, when they are absorbed in learning.  

*Caveat: Attention spans for children at play and when socially engaged will often exceed the maximum figures defined for formal instruction.  

Given today’s technological toys and tools for amusement and productivity, substantial hikes in attention spans correlate with interactive engagement and far exceed traditional figures for normal instructional time spans. Extensions in attention spans are associated with children are  
• challenged (eustress)  
• emotionally involved (“fun”)  
• receiving continuous feedback and support  

Anyone with just a slight degree of experience working with children has observed that when children are completely “immersed in enjoyment,” they often lose track of time and our chart-based expectations are repeatedly shattered.  

Consequently, many American states have recently enacted laws intended to limit the dangerous practice of driving while using a cellular phone (and texting). Even the most dependable statistics on attention spans are meaningless when the brain is sidetracked. The charts presented here are most relevant under optimal conditions in the learning environment. They become skewed once distractions become a factor whether in a car or in a classroom.

Oscar the feline, raised at an elevated care unit for dementia patients at a Rhode Island nursing and rehabilitation center, makes a specialty of visiting the terminally ill. Ordinarily not an extroverted, cuddly feline, Oscar will curl up next to a patient who has mere hours left of life, and purr, purr, purr. from the NEJM article. The feline is more precise by far than any of the doctors, nurses or other human staff at forecasting when it's really time to summon the family to come.  
And as with any cat, a substantial portion of Oscar's days are devoted to zzzzs. He likes to sleep on piles of patient documents. Or on the desk at the nurses' station. Or in the linen closet.  

When alert, however, and strutting about, Oscar the feline projects something very much like the attribute that ancient Romans called gravitas -- a serious commitment to duty.  

"He seems to take very, very earnestly what he does, for whatever reason he does it," said Dosa.

"He only displays great interest in individuals when they are about to pass away," said Dosa.  
(from the Globe article)

AU - da Costa Souza, Patricia Nirlane TI - Aspergillus Biotechnology: An Overview on the Creation of Hydrolases and Secondary Metabolites JO - Current Biotechnology PY - 2017-11-01T00:00:00/// VL - 6 IS - 4 SP - 283 EP - 294 KW - hydrolases KW - secondary metabolites KW - fungal enzymes KW - Aspergillus KW - fungal pigments KW - fungal biotechnology N2 - Background: Microorganisms such as filamentous fungi are significant sources of enzymes and secondary metabolites with broad application in biotechnological processes conducted in various industrial sectors. Aspergillus, one of the most crucial genera of filamentous fungi for this goal, has been utilized as a model to comprehend different biological processes. Despite the presence of some pathogenic Aspergillus strains, many others have been examined from a biotechnological viewpoint.
